tiles.heading: 01 · START AT THE SPATHE
tiles.details:
Flora field cue (Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, p. 1239) — Under Andropogon virginicus, the Flora describes usually straw-colored sheathing bracts around flowering branches 2–3 cm long. Follow several branches to see how they are spaced.

Follow one attached upper culm, not its winter color. Broomsedge is a warm-season tufted perennial; its narrow flowering units are commonly 2–5 short rames per spathe, mostly 1–3 cm long. Panel 1 shows gross flowering hairs, but cannot prove the number or attachment of individual rames.
tiles.short: Several narrow silky racemes are partly tucked into leafy sheaths

tiles.heading: 02 · OPEN ONE SPIKELET PAIR
tiles.details:
Flora field cue (Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, p. 1239) — Find the directly attached spikelet and trace its awn to the lemma. The Flora describes the stalked partner as reduced or absent.

At 10–20× look for a fertile sessile spikelet about 2.5–4 mm and a silky-haired pedicel, usually bearing only a rudiment or no companion spikelet. Identify two enclosing glumes and the thin fertile lemma carrying a straight awn roughly 7–25 mm, depending on treatment. These exact organs are NOT demonstrated by the existing photos; do not arrow hairs as a pedicellate spikelet.

Photo still needed: the pair still attached to its branch, with the reduced companion and its stalk shown in profile.
tiles.short: Fertile sessile spikelet + reduced/absent pedicellate partner

tiles.heading: 03 · OPEN THE TRUE COLLAR
tiles.details: Unfold the blade–sheath junction and photograph the true ciliate membranous ligule beside a 1-mm ruler (published ranges roughly 0.2–1.5 mm). Separate the ligule from hairs on the upper blade or sheath margin. The current gallery does not resolve this structure.
tiles.short: Tiny fringed membrane; variable sheath-edge hairs

tiles.heading: 04 · CHECK LOCAL BLUESTEMS
tiles.details: Anatherum glomeratum forms a broad densely crowded brushlike crown; broomsedge has more separate, narrow spathe-held flowering units. Little bluestem (Schizachyrium scoparium) lacks the same prominent enclosing spathes. Anatherum tenuispatheum requires voucher-based anatomy; do not merge it into bushy bluestem or identify from a fluffy silhouette alone.

tiles.heading: 05 · FINISHING EVIDENCE
tiles.details: To reach public-ready, obtain same-specimen Texas-vouchered rooted growth and complete upper flowering culm (cm scale), opened spathe/rames, true ligule, and dissected paired spikelets, glumes and awned lemma (mm scale). Verify image-level public rights and exact arrows against source pixels, then complete live-site QA. Until then retain FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS.
tiles.short: Rooted plant + measured spathe, ligule and fertile lemma

tiles.heading: 06 · TRACE THE ROOTED CROWN
tiles.details: Follow a flowering culm down to the same rooted bunch. Broomsedge is a perennial bunchgrass rather than a long-rhizomed colony; published culms are roughly 50–110 cm, with commonly 2–5 mm blades. Basal sheaths may be flattened or keeled, but sheath-edge hairs vary and overlap with bushy bluestem. Use the whole plant plus attached spathe-held racemes and measured sessile spikelets, never fall color or one hairy node, to decide. Existing gallery photos show standing culms and leaves but do not prove exposed roots or a dissected collar.
tiles.short: Perennial tuft, often keeled sheaths; winter copper color is not proof
tiles.status: ACTUAL TARGET PHOTO — ROOTS/COLLAR NOT RESOLVED

steps.title: 1 · First, recognize the plant
steps.look_for: Look for narrow silky racemes tucked partly inside flattened spathe-like upper sheaths. Mature plants often turn straw to orange-brown and hold the pale silky seedheads into winter. It does not make the dense brushy crown of bushy bluestem or the digitate turkey foot of big bluestem.
steps.why_it_matters: Start with the recorded recognition characters before making a species identification.

steps.title: 3 · Inspect leaves, collar and nodes
steps.look_for: Unfold the blade–sheath junction and photograph the true ciliate membranous ligule beside a 1-mm ruler (published ranges roughly 0.2–1.5 mm). Separate the ligule from hairs on the upper blade or sheath margin. The current gallery does not resolve this structure.
steps.why_it_matters: Examine the real structures; the photo may not expose or measure all the described characters.

steps.title: 4 · Check the flowering structure
steps.look_for: At 10–20× look for a fertile sessile spikelet about 2.5–4 mm and a silky-haired pedicel, usually bearing only a rudiment or no companion spikelet. Identify two enclosing glumes and the thin fertile lemma carrying a straight awn roughly 7–25 mm, depending on treatment. These exact organs are NOT demonstrated by the existing photos; do not arrow hairs as a pedicellate spikelet.
steps.why_it_matters: Use an attached, correctly identified specimen when deciding the flower or spikelet structures.

steps.title: 5 · Compare similar grasses
steps.look_for: Broomsedge has narrow silky racemes tucked in upper sheaths; bushy bluestem forms a dense brushlike crown, while big bluestem carries a few open turkey-foot racemes.
steps.why_it_matters: Confirm at least two independent botanical characters; do not remove a native candidate from color alone.

panels.label: Broomsedge — silky flowering branch emerging from its sheath
panels.caption: Harry Rose's actual A. virginicus (broomsedge) flowering spathe. The narrow golden leaflike bract runs diagonally above the hand, and a hairy, pale-white flowering branch projects sideways. Photo made in Australia, where the same species is introduced: this does not independently document a native Hays County specimen. The two arrows indicate only visible spathe and silky reproductive branch, not unmeasured sessile/pedicellate spikelets.

panels.label: BROOMSEDGE — mature wind-dispersal unit with radiating silky hairs
panels.caption: Harry Rose CC BY 2.0 photograph of a detached mature broomsedge dispersal unit. Long translucent silky hairs radiate from a narrow central bract structure. The fingertip shows informal scale, not a calibrated ruler. Do not call this individual hair a lemma awn, or the bract a measured glume, without specimen dissection.

panels.label: Broomsedge — detached awned spikelet with silky stalks
panels.caption: Genuine Harry Rose photographed spikelet unit: the central elongated fertile unit bears a long fine awn; curved lateral hairy stalks and reduced sterile partners radiate either side. Actual structures clearly visible. NO printed millimeter reference in frame; do not label exact lemma veins or lengths. Photographer sampled this species in Australia, where it is introduced, NOT a local Texas voucher.

intro: Look for narrow silky racemes tucked partly inside flattened spathe-like upper sheaths. Mature plants often turn straw to orange-brown and hold the pale silky seedheads into winter. It does not make the dense brushy crown of bushy bluestem or the digitate turkey foot of big bluestem.
memory_rule: BROOMSEDGE = more individually separated silky, spathe-held upper racemes; BUSHY = dense clustered terminal brush. A. tenuispatheum is separate accepted species, not just another photo of either.
photo_data_caution: Missing or restricted comparison photographs have not been replaced by guesses. Source statements are not proof the associated structure is visible in any available photo.
